chunks.text: Monarch–Muon: Structure-Aware Muon for Fast and Memory-Efficient Pretraining Alexander Miasnikov 1 , Kabirov Ruslan 1 , Gleb Molodtsov 1 , Dmitrii Vlashchuk 1 , Vladimir Aletov 1 , Nail Bashirov 1 , Daniil Tikhonov 1,2 , Maxim Krutikov 1 , Aleksandr Shestakov 1,3,* , Aleksandr Beznosikov 1 1 BRAIn Lab 2 HSE University 3 MBZUAI * Work performed at BRAIn Lab prior to joining MBZUAI. Code: https://github.com/brain-lab-research/monarch-muon Training large language models is constrained by both wall-clock time and memory footprint, and recent matrix-aware optimizers sharpen this tradeoff: Muon can improve optimization but its dense polar update remains expensive. We propose Monarch–Muon, a structured matrix-aware optimizer for weights parameterized by Monarch factors. The resulting structure reduces weights, gradients, and optimizer state, and exposes small independent update subproblems in place of a single dense orthogonalization; we formalize this through a blockwise trust-region interpretation. In quality runs, Monarch–Muon improves over Monarch–AdamW at fixed structure: 3.06 vs. 3.09 in the dense 257M model and 2.68 vs. 2.77 in the 1B MoE model; the two-block MoE variant also matches dense AdamW while using 15% fewer active and 25.4% fewer total parameters. In 6.89B-parameter systems measurements, Monarch–Muon reduces peak memory from 68.9 to 52.9 GB, Muon optimizer state from 14.60 to 6.77 GB, and the Muon optimizer step from 1288 to 304 ms.

LLM pretraining is a computationally expensive stage of language-model development, where optimization quality, training time, and memory requirements jointly determine the models that can be trained within a given budget. The optimizer affects all three through its update rule, computational cost, and state storage. Therefore, improving optimization must be accompanied by efficient use of memory and hardware. AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) has long been the standard optimizer for large language models. Its coordinatewise updates are inexpensive and straightforward to shard across devices, but its first- and second-moment buffers account for a substantial share of training memory. GaLore ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , APOLLO ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) , and FRUGAL ( Zmushko et al., 2025 ) reduce this storage through compressed statistics or alternative update rules. Such savings can come at the cost of expensive projection operations or slower convergence, while leaving dense weights and gradients unchanged. Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) improves convergence by making an update geometry suited to matrix parameters, while also reducing optimizer state. It replaces coordinatewise adaptation with updates that approximately follow the polar factor of the momentum matrix, corresponding to spectral-norm steepest descent ( Bernstein and Newhouse, 2024 ) . The main cost of Muon is orthogonalization, which involves expensive matrix multiplications and, in sharded implementations, additional communication. Recent methods accelerate polar computation or modify the update and its distributed implementation ( Amsel et al., 2026a ; Khaled et al., 2025 ; Ahn et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . While these advances make matrix-aware updates cheaper, they retain dense weights and gradients.

The parameterization itself offers another route to efficiency. Reducing the number of trainable parameters reduces weights, gradients, and optimizer buffers together. For Muon, a suitable structure can also replace large orthogonalization problems with smaller ones. The important question is whether this computationally cheaper representation retains the optimization benefit of matrix-aware updates. Monarch–Muon uses four blocks and reduces both optimizer-state memory and optimizer-step overhead. We introduce Monarch–Muon, which parameterizes selected weights with Monarch factors ( Dao et al., 2022 ) and applies Muon directly to their trainable blocks. This representation uses fewer parameters while retaining the ability to express full-rank transformations, reducing storage for weights, gradients, and optimizer state. The smaller blocks also make Muon’s orthogonalization cheaper. In dense and mixture-of-experts pretraining, Muon improves validation loss over AdamW at fixed Monarch structure. Systems measurements show that the computational savings grow with matrix size, making the approach particularly effective at larger scales.

Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) demonstrates that changing the update geometry can improve language-model training without maintaining coordinatewise second moments. Its polar update corresponds to spectral-norm steepest descent ( Bernstein and Newhouse, 2024 ) . However, computing spectral updates remains costly for large matrices. The Polar Express ( Amsel et al., 2026a ) and Gram Newton–Schulz ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) reduce the cost of polar approximation. NorMuon ( Li et al., 2026 ) further improves optimization by combining orthogonalization with neuron-wise scaling. Sharded training introduces another obstacle: dense orthogonalization can require communication beyond the local parameter shard. Dion ( Ahn et al., 2025 ) addresses this through low-rank orthonormalized updates with error feedback. MuonBP ( Khaled et al., 2025 ) instead orthogonalizes shards independently and periodically performs full orthogonalization. DMuon ( Chen et al., 2026 ) improves distributed execution, while Dion3 ( Amsel et al., 2026b ) combines efficient kernels, megabatching, and partial orthogonalization. Their trainable weights remain dense, leaving an opportunity to reduce storage and computation through the parameterization itself.

A complementary line reduces the state associated with dense parameters. GaLore ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) stores optimizer statistics in low-rank gradient subspaces, substantially reducing memory. However, projection maintenance adds computation, and restricting updates to these subspaces can discard useful gradient directions. APOLLO ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) uses random projections to approximate adaptive scaling without costly SVD computations. Fira ( Chen et al., 2025 ) extends low-rank adaptive scaling to full-rank gradients, while FRUGAL ( Zmushko et al., 2025 ) combines stateful updates in selected directions with state-free updates in the remainder. These advances improve the memory–quality tradeoff of optimizer-state compression, but retain dense weights and gradients.

Monarch ( Dao et al., 2022 ) provides such a representation through products of block-diagonal factors and permutations. It supports full-rank transformations with fewer parameters and demonstrates efficient training of structured models. Compute Better Spent ( Qiu et al., 2024 ) extends the study of structured layers, including Monarch and block tensor-train matrices, and shows that their performance depends strongly on suitable initialization and learning-rate scaling. Thus, choosing an efficient representation also raises a question: how should its factors be updated? Factorized adaptation methods address a related question for pretrained models. LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) reduces trainable parameters through low-rank updates, while LoRA-Muon ( Cesista et al., 2026 ) develops spectral steepest descent for that low-rank setting. Monarch–Muon targets pretraining with full-rank-capable structured weights. It applies matrix-aware updates directly to the Monarch blocks, using the same structure to reduce training storage and localize orthogonalization. Figure 1 illustrates the resulting savings in training-step time and optimizer-state memory at the largest benchmark scale.

We make the following contributions: • Monarch–Muon optimizer. We introduce Monarch–Muon, a matrix-aware optimizer built on the Monarch parameterization, which reduces weight, gradient, and optimizer-state storage and replaces dense orthogonalization with smaller independent computations. • Theoretical analysis. We derive a blockwise linear-minimization decomposition and prove convergence of exact-polar Monarch–Muon under generalized smoothness. • Experimental validation. Monarch–Muon improves validation loss over Monarch–AdamW in dense and MoE pretraining, matching dense AdamW in MoE with 15% fewer active and 25.4% fewer total parameters. Large-scale benchmarks show 54% lower optimizer-state memory and 45% shorter training steps than dense Muon. • Initialization analysis. To our knowledge, we provide the first systematic study of dense-to-Monarch initialization for SFT, showing that activation-aware fitting and orthogonal rotations improve post-SFT quality over closed-form weight projection under both AdamW and Muon.

Holding the Monarch factorization fixed isolates the effect of the optimizer. We compare AdamW and Muon with two and four blocks, using the same token budget and training schedule within each architecture. Dense AdamW, dense Muon, and GaLore provide reference losses for the dense quality model. The MoE comparison retains the same routing architecture and changes only the selected projections and their optimizer. Monarch–Muon achieves lower final validation loss than Monarch–AdamW in all four structured comparisons (Table 1 ). The two-block MoE reaches the reported loss of dense AdamW with 15% fewer active parameters and 25.4% fewer total parameters (767M versus 1.029B). Figure 2 places this endpoint in the training trajectory. Thus, matrix-aware updates remain useful when the optimizer acts on structured factors rather than dense weights. Increasing the block count further reduces storage, with a higher final loss under both optimizers. Dense Muon gives the lowest loss in each architecture, defining the quality reference for this representation tradeoff. The learned spectra provide a complementary view of the optimizer effect. At the same block count, Monarch–Muon retains a heavier singular-value tail than Monarch–AdamW in the gate and up projections (Figure 3 ). Similar patterns appear in additional layers and components (Appendix B ). Thus, the change in update geometry reaches the represented matrices, even though orthogonalization is local to their factors.

Structure reduces more than the optimizer state: it also compresses the trainable weights and gradients. For Muon, the smaller blocks additionally reduce the cost of orthogonalization. Section 3.2 derives the distinct scaling laws: square-factor storage decreases as 2 / m 2/m of the dense matrix, while Newton–Schulz arithmetic decreases as 2 / m 2 2/m^{2} , where m m is the block count. We test how these savings translate to allocated memory and wall time across five dense reference sizes, using four-block Monarch models and a common microbatch of four. Table 2 includes both optimizer and full-step measurements. Timings for projection-based methods exclude their periodic projection refreshes. The benefit grows with width because cheaper orthogonalization is increasingly accompanied by cheaper forward and backward passes. At 6.89B, Monarch–Muon reduces the full-step time by 45% and peak memory by 23% relative to dense Muon. Its optimizer step is 4.2 × 4.2\times faster and its state occupies 54% less memory. Figure 1 shows that both the model computations and the optimizer contribute to the full-step reduction. At this scale, Monarch–Muon also has the shortest full step and lowest peak memory among the measured state-efficient methods, even though their optimizer steps alone are cheaper. Compressing the representation therefore changes costs that optimizer-state compression leaves dense.

The smallest model marks the hardware crossover: its reduced optimizer cost does not offset the overhead of executing small factor multiplications, and peak memory is slightly higher than for dense Muon. From the 834M reference onward, Monarch–Muon improves both full-step time and peak memory relative to dense Muon. Pretraining learns within the structured representation from the outset. Converting a dense checkpoint instead requires choosing which transformations to replace and how to initialize their factors. We study these choices on the Muon- and AdamW-trained Moonlight-16B-A3B checkpoints ( Liu et al., 2025 ) and then test initialization followed by SFT on Qwen2.5-7B ( Qwen Team, 2025 ) .

Closed-form Monarch projection ( Dao et al., 2022 ) minimizes weight-reconstruction error for a fixed factorization. Functional sensitivity identifies which layers can be converted with little change to model predictions. Figure 4 measures KL divergence to each original checkpoint after replacing one FFN with its four-block projection. The first dense FFN and the final MoE FFN are substantially more sensitive than the interior MoE layers. Both checkpoints are evaluated at step 42,000 on 32 held-out sequences of 2048 tokens, without retraining (Appendix A.3 ). Weight-projection errors do not capture this variation, and interactions between converted layers require candidate sets to be validated jointly. Appendix A.3 provides the weight-space diagnostics and joint-conversion results. Qwen SFT confirms that the choice of components matters beyond the initial projection. We fine-tune converted models for one epoch on 10,000 examples from the Tulu 3 SFT mixture ( Lambert et al., 2025 ) . We measure response negative log-likelihood (NLL) on held-out test data and select learning rates on a separate validation split. Table 3 separates the effects of layer range and projection type. Converting gate and up projections gives lower post-SFT NLL than converting the full MLP at similar parameter counts, under both optimizers. This ordering persists when gate+up conversion spans more layers and uses fewer parameters than the full-MLP comparison. The choice of transformation therefore matters beyond the total number of factors. In particular, preserving the down projection improves the tested quality–storage tradeoff. Weight-space fitting treats every input direction equally. Activation-aware fitting instead weights the error by the calibration activations. Appendix A.4 reports the weight-space diagnostic motivating this choice. We alternate between the two Monarch factors on 128 calibration examples and select the fit on 32 held-out examples, with the full procedure in Appendix A.4 . Table 4 isolates initialization with the same Monarch-factor shapes. Activation-aware fitting ( Nakamura et al., 2026 ) reduces the layer-output error by 40% and closes 76% of the pre-SFT NLL gap to the dense reference. Its advantage remains after SFT with both AdamW and Muon. Orthogonal rotations ( Grishina et al., 2025 ) improve recovery further, at the additional computation described in Appendix A.4 . The tested permutation search ( Mohamed et al., 2025 ) leaves the initialization unchanged. The consistent ordering before and after SFT identifies preservation of layer outputs as a useful criterion for initializing structured factors. Initialization changes post-SFT loss more than the choice between the two factor optimizers in this ablation. AdamW gives slightly lower loss on the selective conversions of this AdamW-pretrained checkpoint, consistent with the observations on retaining the pretraining optimizer in Liu et al. (2025) . The transfer study therefore complements the pretraining result: matrix-aware updates improve learning from scratch, while selective conversion and activation-aware initialization improve recovery of pretrained functions.

Low precision reduces the bytes and arithmetic cost of the representation that Monarch has already compressed. Following the FP8 approach of COAT ( Xi et al., 2025 ) , we evaluate two separate extensions of the two-block dense quality model: FP8 factor GEMMs with compressed activations, and FP8 optimizer buffers with BF16 GEMMs. Both use the same 39,250-step training recipe, with final loss evaluated in BF16 (Appendix A.5 ). The FP8 computation and activation recipe preserves the optimizer ordering while reducing peak memory by about 31% and training-step time by 14% for Monarch–Muon. Final loss remains within 0.23% of BF16 for both optimizers (Table 5 ). Quantizing optimizer buffers separately gives nearly unchanged loss and reduces their storage by 3.7 × 3.7\times . These results show two complementary uses of low precision: reducing the larger activation footprint and further compressing the already smaller optimizer state. Monarch–Muon combines a full-rank-capable structured representation with blockwise matrix-aware updates. This reduces weight, gradient, and optimizer-state storage and replaces dense orthogonalization with smaller independent computations. Our exact-polar analysis gives a convergence guarantee under generalized smoothness. In dense and MoE pretraining, Muon improves loss at fixed Monarch structure, with the two-block MoE matching the reported dense AdamW loss using fewer parameters. Systems measurements show increasing full-step savings at larger widths, complemented by FP8. Dense-checkpoint conversion benefits from jointly selecting components and initializing factors to preserve layer outputs.

Efficiency depends on matrix shape, block count, and kernel execution, motivating sensitivity-guided block allocation and batched low-precision kernels. Complete pretraining at controlled scales and systems measurements at larger widths provide complementary evidence. Longer distributed runs would test their joint quality and hardware tradeoff. Analysis of finite Newton–Schulz updates would connect the exact-polar guarantee to practical orthogonalization.
